subject: MATHS
name: Mensuration
summary: Areas of the awkward shapes, and the surfaces and volumes of solids.
source: NCERT Class 8 Mathematics, syllabus topic coverage only

questions.stem: What is the formula for the area of a trapezium?
choices: ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × height
questions.solution: A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides. Its area is half their sum multiplied by the perpendicular distance between them. The reason is worth seeing: two identical trapeziums placed together form a parallelogram whose base is the sum of the parallel sides, so one trapezium is half of that.

questions.stem: Which quantity is measured in cubic units?
questions.solution: Volume measures how much space a solid occupies, so it needs three lengths multiplied together — hence cubic units such as cm³ or m³. Area needs two, giving square units, and perimeter and height are single lengths. Checking the units of your answer is the fastest way to catch a wrong formula.

questions.stem: Find the area of a trapezium whose parallel sides are 10 cm and 6 cm and whose height is 5 cm.
questions.solution: Area = ½ × (10 + 6) × 5 = ½ × 16 × 5 = 40 cm². The most common mistake is forgetting the half and answering 80. Add the parallel sides first, then halve, then multiply by the height — in that order it is hard to lose a step.

questions.stem: A rhombus has diagonals of 12 cm and 8 cm. What is its area?
questions.solution: The area of a rhombus is half the product of its diagonals: ½ × 12 × 8 = 48 cm². This works because the diagonals of a rhombus cut each other at right angles, dividing it into four right triangles that reassemble into a rectangle of half the size.

questions.stem: What is the total surface area of a cube of side 5 cm?
questions.solution: A cube has 6 identical square faces, each of area 5 × 5 = 25 cm². So the total surface area is 6 × 25 = 150 cm². The distractor 125 is the VOLUME (5³), which is the classic confusion — surface area is measured in cm² and volume in cm³, so the units tell you which you have computed.

questions.stem: Find the volume of a cuboid measuring 8 cm × 5 cm × 3 cm.
questions.solution: Volume of a cuboid = length × breadth × height = 8 × 5 × 3 = 120 cm³. The order does not matter, since multiplication is commutative — which is another way of saying it does not matter which face you stand the box on.

questions.stem: Find the curved surface area of a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. (Take π = 22/7)
questions.solution: Curved surface area = 2πrh = 2 × (22/7) × 7 × 10. The 7 in the radius cancels the 7 in the denominator, leaving 2 × 22 × 10 = 440 cm². Radii of 7, 14 and 21 are chosen in questions precisely so this cancellation happens — spotting it saves the whole calculation.

questions.stem: Find the volume of a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. (Take π = 22/7)
questions.solution: Volume = πr²h = (22/7) × 7 × 7 × 10. One 7 cancels the denominator, leaving 22 × 7 × 10 = 1540 cm³. Compare this with the curved surface area of the same cylinder, 440 cm²: same solid, different question, and the units are what stop you handing in one for the other.

questions.stem: A cuboidal tank measures 2 m × 1.5 m × 1 m. What is its capacity in litres?
questions.solution: Volume = 2 × 1.5 × 1 = 3 m³. The conversion is the whole question: 1 m³ = 1000 litres, so 3 m³ = 3000 litres. It helps to see why — 1 m³ is 100 cm × 100 cm × 100 cm = 1,000,000 cm³, and 1 litre is 1000 cm³.

questions.stem: A cube of side 6 cm is cut into cubes of side 1 cm. How many small cubes are produced?
questions.solution: The large cube has volume 6 × 6 × 6 = 216 cm³, and each small cube has volume 1 cm³, so there are 216 of them. Equivalently, you get 6 along each edge, so 6 × 6 × 6. The distractor 36 is the number on one face, which is what you get if you stop after two dimensions.

questions.stem: The area of a trapezium is 480 cm² and its parallel sides are 20 cm and 12 cm. What is its height?
questions.solution: Work the formula backwards. Area = ½ × (20 + 12) × h, so 480 = ½ × 32 × h = 16h, giving h = 480 ÷ 16 = 30 cm. Rearranging before substituting is safer than substituting and then rearranging: it keeps the halving in one place instead of two.

questions.stem: A rectangular sheet of paper 44 cm long and 20 cm wide is rolled along its length to form a cylinder. What is the volume of the cylinder? (Take π = 22/7)
questions.solution: Rolling along the length means the 44 cm side becomes the circumference of the circular base, and the 20 cm side becomes the height. So 2πr = 44, giving 2 × (22/7) × r = 44 and r = 7 cm. Then volume = πr²h = (22/7) × 7 × 7 × 20 = 3080 cm³. The step that decides the whole answer is the first one — identifying which side wraps round and which stands up.
